access-control-agent.name: access-control-agent
access-control-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits permission models. Map the complete access control surface, then exploit every gap: unprotected functions, escalation chains, broken initialization, inconsistent guards.

asymmetry-agent.name: asymmetry-agent
asymmetry-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits asymmetries — between paired functions, between branches within a function, and between writers and readers of the same storage variable. The bug is not in one wrong line; it's in what's missing or different across two places that should match.

boundary-agent.name: boundary-agent
boundary-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits the gap between assumed and actual behavior at external boundaries. Your method is disciplined enumeration: walk every call site, every branch, every input source, and apply a fixed set of corner-case questions to each.

economic-security-agent.name: economic-security-agent
economic-security-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits external dependencies, value flows, and economic incentives. You have unlimited capital and flash loans. Every dependency failure, token misbehavior, and misaligned incentive is an extraction opportunity.

execution-trace-agent.name: execution-trace-agent
execution-trace-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits execution flow — tracing from entry point to final state through encoding, storage, branching, external calls, and state transitions. Every place the code assumes something about execution that isn't enforced is your opportunity.

first-principles-agent.name: first-principles-agent
first-principles-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits what others can't even name. Ignore known vulnerability patterns entirely — read the code's own logic, identify every implicit assumption, and systematically violate them.

flow-gap-agent.name: flow-gap-agent
flow-gap-agent.description: You are an attacker that hunts bugs in the GAPS between three control-flow lenses: execution trace (where control actually goes), periphery (external touchpoints — tokens, oracles, callbacks, low-level calls), and first principles (what the protocol is fundamentally supposed to do).

invariant-agent.name: invariant-agent
invariant-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits broken invariants — conservation laws, state couplings, and equivalence relationships. Map what must stay true, find the code path that violates it, and extract value from the broken state.

math-precision-agent.name: math-precision-agent
math-precision-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits integer arithmetic: rounding errors, precision loss, decimal mismatches, overflow, and scale mixing. Every truncation, every wrong rounding direction, every unchecked cast is an extraction opportunity.

numerical-gap-agent.name: numerical-gap-agent
numerical-gap-agent.description: You are an attacker that hunts bugs in the GAPS between three numerical lenses: precision (rounding/scale/truncation), invariants (mathematical properties that should hold), and boundaries (edges, zeros, max values).

periphery-agent.name: periphery-agent
periphery-agent.description: You are an attacker that exploits the code nobody else is looking at — libraries, helpers, encoders, utilities, base contracts. Core contracts trust this code implicitly. One bug in a 20-line library compromises every caller.

shared-rules.name: shared-rules
shared-rules.description: Your bundle is four concatenated files: all in-scope source code, the SOP (HOW to think), your specialty agent (WHAT to look for), and these shared rules (output format, dedup tags, AND mandatory mental tool protocol).

trust-gap-agent.name: trust-gap-agent
trust-gap-agent.description: You are an attacker that hunts bugs in the GAPS between three trust lenses: access control (who is allowed), economic security (who profits/pays), and asymmetry (who is treated differently from whom).

judging.name: judging
judging.description: Every finding passes four sequential gates. Fail any gate → rejected or demoted to lead. Later gates are not evaluated for failed findings.

report-formatting.name: report-formatting
report-formatting.description: Save the report to {project-name}-pashov-ai-audit-report-{timestamp}.md in the current working directory, where {project-name} is the repo root basename and {timestamp} is YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS at scan time.

senior-auditor-sop.name: senior-auditor-sop
senior-auditor-sop.description: This is how a senior auditor thinks. Pattern-matching catches the obvious bugs — your specialty file teaches that. The high-value bugs, the ones everyone else misses, come from HOW you reason about code, not from WHAT bugs you know.

templates.name: templates
templates.description: Write x-ray.md using this exact structure. Every line should tell an auditor something useful — write for someone who has 5 minutes to decide where to look first.

threats.name: threats
threats.description: HOW TO USE THIS FILE Treat this file as a threat identification library, not as a prose template for the final report. - In Step 2e (Protocol Classification) — use the detection-signals table to label the protocol by type. - In Step 3a (Writing Section 2 of x-ray.md) — use adversary rankings, attack

anchor-checks.name: anchor-checks
anchor-checks.description: - Check if PDA derivations use all required seeds and verify bump seeds are canonical - Look for CPI calls that don't validate the target program ID matches expected program - Verify if account validation checks both owner and discriminator for all account types - Search for instructions that don't

finding-format.name: finding-format
finding-format.description: FINDING FORMAT: Ensure findings created follow this format very strictly:

move-checks.name: move-checks
move-checks.description: - Check every function accepting Coin<T or generic <T - confirm T is validated against a whitelist or phantom type constraint on the container; unvalidated generics are the number-one critical finding in real Move audits - Search for public(package) entry or public entry function declarations - entr

multi-expert.name: multi-expert
multi-expert.description: EXECUTION INSTRUCTION: You must perform THREE SEPARATE ANALYSIS ROUNDS, adopting a completely different persona and approach for each expert. Do not blend their perspectives - maintain strict separation between each expert's analysis.

fv-anc-1-cl1-overflow-underflow-in-arith.name: fv-anc-1-cl1-overflow-underflow-in-arithmetic-operations
fv-anc-1-cl1-overflow-underflow-in-arith.description: Integer overflow and underflow in Rust Anchor programs occur when arithmetic on u64/u128/i64 values wraps or panics, leading to corrupted balances, bypassed caps, or exploitable logic. In release builds, Rust integers wrap silently unless checked variants are used.

fv-anc-1-cl2-division-by-zero.name: fv-anc-1-cl2-division-by-zero
fv-anc-1-cl2-division-by-zero.description: Division by zero in an Anchor instruction causes a panic and transaction failure. When the divisor is derived from user-supplied input or an account field, an attacker can trigger a denial-of-service by passing zero.

fv-anc-1-cl3-arbitrary-rounding.name: fv-anc-1-cl3-arbitrary-rounding
fv-anc-1-cl3-arbitrary-rounding.description: Inconsistent or unintended rounding in fixed-point arithmetic causes cumulative loss or gain of funds. In Anchor programs handling token amounts or exchange rates, the choice of floor, ceiling, or round-to-nearest has protocol-level security implications.

fv-anc-1-cl4-saturating-math-misuse-in-f.name: fv-anc-1-cl4-saturating-math-misuse-in-financial-contexts
fv-anc-1-cl4-saturating-math-misuse-in-f.description: Using .saturatingadd() or .saturatingsub() in financial contexts silently caps values at u64::MAX or 0 instead of signaling an error. This masks real overflow or underflow conditions, leaving accounts with corrupted balances that are neither reverted nor flagged, and potentially allowing exploitatio

fv-anc-1-cl5-round-trip-vault-profit-via.name: fv-anc-1-cl5-round-trip-vault-profit-via-precision-gap
fv-anc-1-cl5-round-trip-vault-profit-via.description: A deposit followed by an immediate withdrawal can extract value when share-to-asset conversion rounds in the depositor's favor at both steps. When both mint and redeem paths round down at the asset level, an attacker can systematically drain dust from a vault across many round-trip transactions, par

fv-anc-10-cl1-closing-accounts-without-z.name: fv-anc-10-cl1-closing-accounts-without-zeroing-data-and-setting-a-closed-discriminator
fv-anc-10-cl1-closing-accounts-without-z.description: Manually closing an account by zeroing its lamports without also zeroing its data and writing a closed discriminator leaves the account readable as if still active. An attacker can revive the account within the same transaction or exploit the stale data in subsequent instructions.

fv-anc-10-cl2-operations-on-accounts-mar.name: fv-anc-10-cl2-operations-on-accounts-marked-as-closed
fv-anc-10-cl2-operations-on-accounts-mar.description: An account bearing a closed discriminator should be rejected at the start of any instruction that would read or mutate it. Failing to check allows a closed account to be passed into an instruction and processed as if still valid.

fv-anc-10-cl3-unintended-closure-by-clos.name: fv-anc-10-cl3-unintended-closure-by-close-constraint
fv-anc-10-cl3-unintended-closure-by-clos.description: Anchor's close constraint closes the account and transfers its lamports at the end of the instruction, regardless of what the instruction body does. Applying it to accounts that should only conditionally be closed, or misunderstanding when the closure executes, can lead to unintended data and lampor

fv-anc-11-cl1-missing-slippage-tolerance.name: fv-anc-11-cl1-missing-slippage-tolerance-allowing-extraction
fv-anc-11-cl1-missing-slippage-tolerance.description: Instructions that perform token swaps, liquidity operations, or price-sensitive conversions without a caller-supplied minimum output amount allow extractors to sandwich the transaction. On Solana, MEV via Jito bundles means any public transaction with zero slippage protection is a reliable extractio

fv-anc-11-cl2-lamport-balance-invariant-.name: fv-anc-11-cl2-lamport-balance-invariant-violation-in-cpi
fv-anc-11-cl2-lamport-balance-invariant-.description: Solana programs that perform CPIs can inadvertently violate the lamport conservation invariant: the total lamports across all accounts touched by a transaction must be the same before and after. If a program transfers lamports via a CPI and also modifies account data in ways that change the rent-exe

fv-anc-11-cl3-dust-account-poisoning-blo.name: fv-anc-11-cl3-dust-account-poisoning-blocking-critical-operations
fv-anc-11-cl3-dust-account-poisoning-blo.description: An attacker can send a tiny lamport amount to a program-controlled account, increasing its balance above the rent-exempt minimum for zero bytes but below what a later close or realloc operation expects. This can cause close constraints to fail (because balance != expected), leave accounts in an un-c

fv-anc-11-cl4-unbounded-account-collecti.name: fv-anc-11-cl4-unbounded-account-collection-causing-dos
fv-anc-11-cl4-unbounded-account-collecti.description: Instructions that iterate over a variable-length collection stored in an account (a Vec of positions, orders, or members) can exhaust compute units when the collection grows large. An attacker can repeatedly add entries to grow the collection to a size that makes all dependent instructions fail due

fv-anc-11-cl5-time-unit-mismatch-in-dead.name: fv-anc-11-cl5-time-unit-mismatch-in-deadline-validation
fv-anc-11-cl5-time-unit-mismatch-in-dead.description: Solana's Clock sysvar provides both unixtimestamp (seconds since Unix epoch) and slot (current slot number). Mixing these two units in deadline or expiry comparisons produces incorrect results: a value stored in seconds interpreted as a slot number, or vice versa, can make a deadline that should exp

fv-anc-11-cl6-reward-accumulator-updated.name: fv-anc-11-cl6-reward-accumulator-updated-after-balance-change
fv-anc-11-cl6-reward-accumulator-updated.description: Staking and reward protocols that track per-share reward accumulation must update the global accumulator index before modifying any user's share balance. If the index is updated after a deposit or withdrawal, the user's new balance is used to calculate their retroactive entitlement to rewards that a

fv-anc-13-cl1-compute-budget-dos-via-use.name: fv-anc-13-cl1-compute-budget-dos-via-user-injected-limit-instruction
fv-anc-13-cl1-compute-budget-dos-via-use.description: Solana transactions can include a SetComputeUnitLimit instruction that caps the compute units available for the entire transaction. A malicious user can prepend a SetComputeUnitLimit with a very low value before calling a protocol instruction, causing the instruction to exhaust compute units and fai

fv-anc-13-cl2-uninitialized-vec-capacity.name: fv-anc-13-cl2-uninitialized-vec-capacity-bug
fv-anc-13-cl2-uninitialized-vec-capacity.description: Creating a Vec with Vec::withcapacity(n) allocates space for n elements but leaves the length at 0. Accessing elements of a capacity-allocated but not length-populated Vec via index operators will produce an out-of-bounds panic. If an initialization instruction fails to push actual elements and a su

fv-anc-13-cl3-upgrade-authority-not-tran.name: fv-anc-13-cl3-upgrade-authority-not-transferred-or-locked
fv-anc-13-cl3-upgrade-authority-not-tran.description: Anchor programs deployed with a live upgrade authority can be modified by the authority holder at any time without on-chain governance or timelock. If the upgrade authority is a single keypair rather than a multisig or locked to None, a key compromise or insider action can replace the program binary

fv-anc-13-cl4-log-truncation-hiding-crit.name: fv-anc-13-cl4-log-truncation-hiding-critical-security-events
fv-anc-13-cl4-log-truncation-hiding-crit.description: Solana transactions are limited in total compute units per transaction. When a program emits extensive logs near the compute limit, the Solana runtime truncates log output silently. Security-critical events emitted near or after the compute budget is exhausted will not appear in the transaction logs

fv-anc-2-cl1-unvalidated-signers.name: fv-anc-2-cl1-unvalidated-signers
fv-anc-2-cl1-unvalidated-signers.description: Declaring an account as AccountInfo<'info rather than Signer<'info in an Anchor context struct means the framework does not enforce that the account signed the transaction. Any public key can be passed as the authority without authorization.

fv-anc-2-cl2-no-is-signer-check.name: fv-anc-2-cl2-no-is-signer-check
fv-anc-2-cl2-no-is-signer-check.description: When using raw AccountInfo or native Solana program patterns, the issigner field on the account info must be explicitly checked. Omitting this check means an instruction accepts any account as an authority without verifying it signed the transaction.

fv-anc-3-cl1-trying-to-modify-an-account.name: fv-anc-3-cl1-trying-to-modify-an-account-without-checking-if-its-writeable
fv-anc-3-cl1-trying-to-modify-an-account.description: Solana requires accounts to be marked writable in the transaction's account list before the runtime permits lamport or data changes. Writing to an account not flagged as writable will either panic or silently fail depending on the Solana version, and opens logic errors when the writability check is

fv-anc-3-cl10-using-ctx-remaining-accoun.name: fv-anc-3-cl10-using-ctx-remaining-accounts-without-non-zero-data-check
fv-anc-3-cl10-using-ctx-remaining-accoun.description: An uninitialized account on Solana has all-zero data. Accepting such an account from ctx.remainingaccounts without checking that it contains non-zero data allows an attacker to pass an empty system account that will be deserialized as a zero-value struct, potentially bypassing balance or state check

fv-anc-3-cl11-no-reload-after-account-mu.name: fv-anc-3-cl11-no-reload-after-account-mutation
fv-anc-3-cl11-no-reload-after-account-mu.description: In Anchor, after mutating an account via a loadmut() or direct field write, subsequent reads of the same account may use a stale in-memory copy. Without explicitly reloading, the program may act on outdated state, leading to logic errors when the mutation affects values read later in the same instru

fv-anc-3-cl12-not-validating-a-set-addre.name: fv-anc-3-cl12-not-validating-a-set-address
fv-anc-3-cl12-not-validating-a-set-addre.description: When an instruction stores a new address into an account field (e.g., updating a treasury, fee recipient, or authority), failing to validate that address allows arbitrary pubkeys to be set. This can redirect funds, grant privileges to attacker-controlled accounts, or break protocol invariants.

fv-anc-3-cl13-init-if-needed-without-rei.name: fv-anc-3-cl13-init-if-needed-without-reinit-guard
fv-anc-3-cl13-init-if-needed-without-rei.description: Anchor's initifneeded skips account creation if the account already exists, but it does not prevent an attacker from pre-creating the PDA with malicious initial state. Without a reinitialization guard in the instruction body, a subsequent call that skips init will silently operate on attacker-contro

fv-anc-3-cl14-realloc-without-zero-init.name: fv-anc-3-cl14-realloc-without-zero-init
fv-anc-3-cl14-realloc-without-zero-init.description: Anchor's realloc constraint expands an account's data allocation. When realloc::zeroinit = false, newly exposed bytes from the previous allocation are not zeroed and may contain stale data from prior account usage. Reading those bytes as structured fields yields unpredictable values.

fv-anc-3-cl2-trying-to-access-account-da.name: fv-anc-3-cl2-trying-to-access-account-data-without-ownership-checks
fv-anc-3-cl2-trying-to-access-account-da.description: On Solana, any account can be passed to a program. Without verifying that an account is owned by the expected program, an attacker can substitute a look-alike account controlled by a different program, causing the instruction to operate on attacker-crafted data.

fv-anc-3-cl3-usage-of-uncheckedaccount-w.name: fv-anc-3-cl3-usage-of-uncheckedaccount-without-manual-ownership-check
fv-anc-3-cl3-usage-of-uncheckedaccount-w.description: UncheckedAccount<'info explicitly bypasses Anchor's automatic ownership and discriminator verification. Any instruction using this type must manually perform the ownership checks that Account<'info, T would otherwise enforce, or an attacker can supply an account owned by any program.

fv-anc-3-cl4-usage-of-uncheckedaccount-w.name: fv-anc-3-cl4-usage-of-uncheckedaccount-without-manual-signer-check
fv-anc-3-cl4-usage-of-uncheckedaccount-w.description: When UncheckedAccount<'info is used for an account that is expected to authorize an action, the issigner field must be explicitly checked in the instruction body. Anchor does not perform this check automatically for unchecked account types.

fv-anc-3-cl5-no-is-initialized-check-whe.name: fv-anc-3-cl5-no-is-initialized-check-when-operating-on-an-account
fv-anc-3-cl5-no-is-initialized-check-whe.description: Operating on an uninitialized account allows instructions to read garbage data or overwrite state during initialization with attacker-controlled values. Anchor's [account(init)] guards against double-initialization, but manually managed accounts or legacy patterns that track initialization via a boo

fv-anc-3-cl6-missing-account-constraints.name: fv-anc-3-cl6-missing-account-constraints
fv-anc-3-cl6-missing-account-constraints.description: Anchor constraints such as hasone, constraint, and address enforce relational correctness between accounts at the framework level. Omitting these constraints forces the instruction body to perform manual checks, and if those checks are also absent, an attacker can pass unrelated accounts.

fv-anc-3-cl7-duplicate-mutable-accounts.name: fv-anc-3-cl7-duplicate-mutable-accounts
fv-anc-3-cl7-duplicate-mutable-accounts.description: When two mutable account fields in an Anchor context can be satisfied by the same public key, an attacker can pass the same account for both. Instructions that assume the accounts are distinct (e.g., transferring between them) will produce incorrect results or allow double-mutation exploits.

fv-anc-3-cl8-using-ctx-remaining-account.name: fv-anc-3-cl8-using-ctx-remaining-accounts-without-manual-ownership-check
fv-anc-3-cl8-using-ctx-remaining-account.description: ctx.remainingaccounts provides raw AccountInfo references with no Anchor-enforced constraints. Every account taken from this slice must be manually validated for ownership before its data is read or it is passed to a CPI, otherwise an attacker can substitute an account owned by any program.

fv-anc-3-cl9-using-ctx-remaining-account.name: fv-anc-3-cl9-using-ctx-remaining-accounts-without-manual-discriminator-check
fv-anc-3-cl9-using-ctx-remaining-account.description: Accounts from ctx.remainingaccounts bypass Anchor's automatic discriminator verification. Without checking the first 8 bytes against the expected Anchor discriminator, an attacker can pass an account of a different struct type that shares the same owner program, leading to type confusion.

fv-anc-4-cl1-using-create-program-addres.name: fv-anc-4-cl1-using-create-program-address
fv-anc-4-cl1-using-create-program-addres.description: Pubkey::createprogramaddress requires a caller-supplied bump seed and does not find the canonical bump. An attacker can supply a non-canonical bump that produces a valid but unintended PDA, bypassing seed-based access controls or creating collisions with legitimate PDAs.

fv-anc-4-cl2-pda-seed-concatenation-coll.name: fv-anc-4-cl2-pda-seed-concatenation-collision
fv-anc-4-cl2-pda-seed-concatenation-coll.description: When multiple variable-length byte slices are passed as PDA seeds without length disambiguation, different combinations of inputs can produce the same raw seed bytes and therefore the same PDA address. An attacker can craft inputs that collide with a legitimate account's PDA.

fv-anc-4-cl3-pda-sharing-single-global-v.name: fv-anc-4-cl3-pda-sharing-single-global-vault
fv-anc-4-cl3-pda-sharing-single-global-v.description: A vault PDA derived from constant seeds (e.g., only b"vault") is shared across all users or positions. Compromising any single user's position, or exploiting any instruction that touches the vault, can drain funds belonging to all other users.

fv-anc-4-cl4-pda-purpose-isolation-failu.name: fv-anc-4-cl4-pda-purpose-isolation-failure
fv-anc-4-cl4-pda-purpose-isolation-failu.description: When different instruction handlers derive PDAs using identical or overlapping seed sets, an attacker can substitute one PDA in place of another. Instructions that accept a PDA account by key alone without validating its discriminator or type-specific field allow cross-context injection, enabling an

fv-anc-4-cl5-pda-signer-without-ownershi.name: fv-anc-4-cl5-pda-signer-without-ownership-verification
fv-anc-4-cl5-pda-signer-without-ownershi.description: Using invokesigned with PDA seeds to authorize a CPI without first verifying the PDA account is owned by the calling program allows a forged PDA from a different program to authorize operations it should not perform. If two programs can derive the same address from the same seeds, the legitimate pro

fv-anc-5-cl1-lack-of-validation-of-exter.name: fv-anc-5-cl1-lack-of-validation-of-external-program-before-cpi
fv-anc-5-cl1-lack-of-validation-of-exter.description: When the program ID for a CPI target is passed as an account in the transaction rather than hardcoded, an attacker can substitute a malicious program. Without validating the program ID before calling, the CPI executes arbitrary attacker-controlled code with the caller's account context.

fv-anc-5-cl10-cross-program-reentrancy-v.name: fv-anc-5-cl10-cross-program-reentrancy-via-callback
fv-anc-5-cl10-cross-program-reentrancy-v.description: Solana's CPI depth limit does not prevent reentrancy when program A calls program B which calls back into program A at a different instruction before A's state is finalized. Unlike EVM, there is no automatic reentrancy guard at the runtime level; account state is accessible across CPI hops within th

fv-anc-5-cl11-cpi-to-upgradeable-program.name: fv-anc-5-cl11-cpi-to-upgradeable-program-without-version-pin
fv-anc-5-cl11-cpi-to-upgradeable-program.description: Calling an upgradeable program via CPI exposes the caller to logic changes introduced by the program's upgrade authority. If the calling protocol does not pin the expected program binary hash or validate the upgrade slot, an upgrade to the dependency program can silently change the semantics of the

fv-anc-5-cl2-cpi-without-signer-seeds.name: fv-anc-5-cl2-cpi-without-signer-seeds
fv-anc-5-cl2-cpi-without-signer-seeds.description: When a CPI requires a PDA to sign on behalf of the program, invokesigned must be called with the correct signer seeds. Using invoke or passing empty seeds to invokesigned causes the CPI to fail or to execute without the PDA's authority, breaking the intended access control.

fv-anc-5-cl3-not-unsetting-signer-status.name: fv-anc-5-cl3-not-unsetting-signer-status-before-a-cpi
fv-anc-5-cl3-not-unsetting-signer-status.description: When a user-signed account is passed into a CPI, the callee receives it with issigner = true. A malicious or compromised callee can exploit this elevated status to perform privileged operations on the user's account that the caller did not intend to authorize.

fv-anc-5-cl4-passing-unnecessary-account.name: fv-anc-5-cl4-passing-unnecessary-accounts-to-cpis
fv-anc-5-cl4-passing-unnecessary-account.description: Including accounts in a CPI that the callee does not need expands the trust surface. A malicious callee can read data from, or attempt privileged operations on, any account passed to it. Each unnecessary account increases the blast radius if the callee is compromised or malicious.

fv-anc-5-cl5-sol-balance-drain-via-cpi.name: fv-anc-5-cl5-sol-balance-drain-via-cpi
fv-anc-5-cl5-sol-balance-drain-via-cpi.description: When a program passes an account with a SOL balance to an external program via CPI, the callee can debit lamports from that account if it holds write authority. Without checking the balance before and after the CPI, the caller cannot detect or prevent unexpected lamport drain.

fv-anc-5-cl6-post-cpi-ownership-change.name: fv-anc-5-cl6-post-cpi-ownership-change
fv-anc-5-cl6-post-cpi-ownership-change.description: A callee program can call assign on any account it is authorized to write, changing that account's owner to an arbitrary program. If the caller does not re-verify account ownership after the CPI, it may continue operating on an account now owned by an attacker-controlled program.

fv-anc-5-cl7-invoke-signed-with-wrong-or.name: fv-anc-5-cl7-invoke-signed-with-wrong-or-partial-seeds
fv-anc-5-cl7-invoke-signed-with-wrong-or.description: If the seeds array passed to invokesigned does not exactly match the seeds used to derive the PDA that is expected to sign, the call will fail or sign under the wrong identity. More critically, when multiple seed combinations can resolve to valid program addresses, using an incorrect subset can auth

fv-anc-5-cl8-cpi-to-system-program-creat.name: fv-anc-5-cl8-cpi-to-system-program-creates-unintended-account
fv-anc-5-cl8-cpi-to-system-program-creat.description: A CPI to the system program's createaccount or assign instruction with attacker-influenced parameters can create or reassign accounts at addresses that hold special protocol meaning. If the target address is a protocol PDA, config account, or authority record, the CPI can overwrite or initialize it

fv-anc-5-cl9-cpi-privilege-escalation-vi.name: fv-anc-5-cl9-cpi-privilege-escalation-via-account-authority
fv-anc-5-cl9-cpi-privilege-escalation-vi.description: When accounts passed into a CPI carry iswritable or issigner flags that originated from the outer transaction context, an attacker can escalate privileges inside the CPI by crafting the outer transaction's account flags. Anchor's CpiContext does not automatically strip or re-derive account privilege

fv-anc-6-cl1-unclear-error-messages.name: fv-anc-6-cl1-unclear-error-messages
fv-anc-6-cl1-unclear-error-messages.description: Using generic Solana ProgramError variants instead of custom Anchor error codes makes it impossible for clients, indexers, and auditors to determine why a transaction failed. Opaque errors also impede incident response and make it harder to distinguish security-critical rejections from benign valida

fv-anc-7-cl1-unvalidated-token-mint-and-.name: fv-anc-7-cl1-unvalidated-token-mint-and-owner
fv-anc-7-cl1-unvalidated-token-mint-and-.description: Token accounts on Solana carry a mint and an owner field. Without validating both, an attacker can substitute a token account for a different mint (causing the program to treat the wrong token as the expected asset) or a different owner (allowing unauthorized access to balances).

fv-anc-7-cl2-using-init-with-an-ata.name: fv-anc-7-cl2-using-init-with-an-ata
fv-anc-7-cl2-using-init-with-an-ata.description: Using [account(init, associatedtoken::...)] on a token account fails if the ATA already exists, because init requires the account to be uninitialized. Any user who pre-creates the ATA before the instruction runs triggers a transaction failure, producing a denial-of-service vector.

fv-anc-7-cl3-token-2022-incompatibility.name: fv-anc-7-cl3-token-2022-incompatibility
fv-anc-7-cl3-token-2022-incompatibility.description: The legacy SPL Token program and Token-2022 have different program IDs and different instruction formats for operations like transfer. Code that hardcodes anchorspl::token will fail or behave incorrectly when used with Token-2022 mints, which introduce transfer fees, interest, confidential transfers

fv-anc-7-cl4-token-2022-transfer-hook-by.name: fv-anc-7-cl4-token-2022-transfer-hook-bypass-or-missing
fv-anc-7-cl4-token-2022-transfer-hook-by.description: Token-2022 mints can register a transfer hook program that must be invoked on every token transfer. Programs that use the legacy spltoken::transfer instruction or call the SPL Token program ID directly (TokenkegQfe...) bypass the hook entirely, violating the mint's invariants and potentially enablin

fv-anc-7-cl5-interest-bearing-mint-princ.name: fv-anc-7-cl5-interest-bearing-mint-principal-vs-balance-confusion
fv-anc-7-cl5-interest-bearing-mint-princ.description: Token-2022 interest-bearing mints compound an on-chain rate that increases the displayed token balance over time. Programs that read the raw TokenAccount.amount without calling the extension's amounttouiamount conversion will undercount the actual accrued value, leading to mispriced collateral, inco

fv-anc-7-cl6-transfer-fee-extension-acco.name: fv-anc-7-cl6-transfer-fee-extension-accounting-error
fv-anc-7-cl6-transfer-fee-extension-acco.description: Token-2022 transfer fee extensions deduct a fee from transferred amounts at the SPL level. Programs that send X tokens and expect X tokens to arrive at the destination will undercount the actual received amount. This causes shortfalls in vault deposits, incorrect share issuance, fee revenue discrepa

fv-anc-7-cl7-unconstrained-freeze-author.name: fv-anc-7-cl7-unconstrained-freeze-authority
fv-anc-7-cl7-unconstrained-freeze-author.description: A token account can be frozen by the mint's freeze authority at any time, permanently preventing deposits, withdrawals, and transfers. Protocols that accept tokens from mints where freeze authority has not been revoked expose themselves to an attack or admin error where a malicious or compromised fr

fv-anc-7-cl8-mint-close-authority-exploi.name: fv-anc-7-cl8-mint-close-authority-exploitation
fv-anc-7-cl8-mint-close-authority-exploi.description: Token-2022 mints can define a close authority that can close the mint account entirely and reclaim its rent. fv-anc-8-cl1-unvalidated-sysvar-address.name: fv-anc-8-cl1-unvalidated-sysvar-address
fv-anc-8-cl1-unvalidated-sysvar-address.description: Solana sysvars (Clock, Rent, SlotHashes, etc.) have fixed public addresses. If a sysvar is accepted as an AccountInfo without verifying its address, an attacker can substitute a different account, causing the program to read attacker-controlled data as if it were the sysvar.

fv-anc-8-cl2-instruction-introspection-u.name: fv-anc-8-cl2-instruction-introspection-using-absolute-index
fv-anc-8-cl2-instruction-introspection-u.description: Programs that call loadinstructionatchecked(index, ...) with a hardcoded or fixed index assume a specific transaction layout. An attacker can prepend additional instructions, shifting the intended instruction to a different position and causing the verification to either fail or point at an unrelate

fv-anc-8-cl3-address-lookup-table-signer.name: fv-anc-8-cl3-address-lookup-table-signer-forgery
fv-anc-8-cl3-address-lookup-table-signer.description: Address Lookup Tables (ALTs) expand transaction account lists from compressed indices. A malicious transaction can use an ALT to inject accounts that appear at indices the program expects to belong to specific signers or programs. Programs that identify accounts by position rather than by explicit k

fv-anc-8-cl4-durable-nonce-transaction-o.name: fv-anc-8-cl4-durable-nonce-transaction-ordering-attack
fv-anc-8-cl4-durable-nonce-transaction-o.description: Durable nonce transactions replace the recentblockhash field with a nonce value that does not expire with slots, allowing a signed transaction to be submitted at any future time. Protocols that rely on transaction recency for security (signed price updates, authority transfers, time-bounded operatio

fv-anc-9-cl1-not-using-discriminators-to.name: fv-anc-9-cl1-not-using-discriminators-to-validate-account-types
fv-anc-9-cl1-not-using-discriminators-to.description: Anchor automatically prepends an 8-byte discriminator to every [account] struct. When deserializing accounts manually or accepting them via UncheckedAccount, failing to check the discriminator allows an attacker to pass an account of a different type that happens to have the same owner program, caus

fv-anc-9-cl2-account-structures-without-.name: fv-anc-9-cl2-account-structures-without-discriminators
fv-anc-9-cl2-account-structures-without-.description: Account structs defined without Anchor's [account] attribute do not receive an automatic 8-byte discriminator. This means all instances of such structs look identical at the byte level regardless of their intended type, enabling type substitution attacks across any instruction that accepts them.

amm-dex.name: amm-dex
amm-dex.description: Applies to: Dedust-style AMM protocols, STON.fi-style swap contracts, liquidity pool contracts on TON, swap routers, Jetton-based liquidity pools, any FunC or Tact contract implementing constant-product or curve-based invariant math, position managers, concentrated liquidity implementations

governance.name: governance
governance.description: Applies to: DAO governance, on-chain voting, governance token voting, timelocks, proposal execution, treasury management, Compound Governor-style, OpenZeppelin Governor-style

lending.name: lending
lending.description: Applies to: TON lending protocols, collateralized borrowing contracts, vault share protocols, Jetton-based money markets, stablecoin CDPs, over-collateralized loan contracts, flash loan providers, any FunC or Tact contract that issues shares against deposited Jetton or TON collateral

oracle.name: oracle
oracle.description: Applies to: TON lending collateral pricing, TON derivatives and perpetuals, synthetic asset minting, margin trading contracts, any FunC or Tact contract consuming external price data on TON, Pyth on TON integrations, Redstone on TON, off-chain oracle with on-chain delivery

staking.name: staking
staking.description: Applies to: TON nominator pool contracts, validator delegation protocols, liquid staking on TON, Jetton-based staking reward distributors, TON Whales staking, tsTON, hTON, any FunC or Tact contract distributing rewards proportional to staked balances over time

fv-mov-1-cl1-copy-ability-duplication.name: fv-mov-1-cl1-copy-ability-duplication
fv-mov-1-cl1-copy-ability-duplication.description: A value-bearing object (coin, NFT, badge, receipt, staking position) granted the copy ability can be duplicated by any holder. The attacker duplicates a token to drain pools, inflate supply, or repeatedly spend the same credential.

fv-mov-1-cl2-drop-ability-debt-destructi.name: fv-mov-1-cl2-drop-ability-debt-destruction
fv-mov-1-cl2-drop-ability-debt-destructi.description: An obligation object (flash loan receipt, debt record, collateral lock, vesting lock) granted the drop ability can be silently discarded. A borrower drops the receipt without repaying; a collateral lock is dropped to unlock assets early.

fv-mov-1-cl3-store-ability-wrapping.name: fv-mov-1-cl3-store-ability-wrapping
fv-mov-1-cl3-store-ability-wrapping.description: A sensitive object (AdminCap, TreasuryCap, UpgradeCap) granted the store ability can be wrapped inside any other object and transferred out of the protocol's visibility. The attacker wraps the capability into a custom container and transfers it to an address they control, bypassing transfer policies

fv-mov-1-cl4-object-wrapping-lock.name: fv-mov-1-cl4-object-wrapping-lock
fv-mov-1-cl4-object-wrapping-lock.description: A contract wraps a user-owned object inside its own struct (or dynamic field) and provides no guaranteed path to unwrap it. Once wrapped, the inner object loses its independent identity - it cannot be transferred, used, or accessed until explicitly unwrapped by the wrapping contract. If the wrapping

fv-mov-2-cl1-missing-capability-check.name: fv-mov-2-cl1-missing-capability-check
fv-mov-2-cl1-missing-capability-check.description: A function that performs admin or privileged operations (withdraw, mint, pause, config update) does not require a capability object parameter. Any user can call the function and perform admin operations without restriction.

fv-mov-2-cl2-capability-lifecycle.name: fv-mov-2-cl2-capability-lifecycle
fv-mov-2-cl2-capability-lifecycle.description: Capability objects (AdminCap, TreasuryCap) should be created only once during module initialization (init). Creating them in any other function, without requiring an existing capability, allows any caller to mint new admin credentials. Similarly, coins created without the one-time witness (OTW) patt

fv-mov-2-cl3-entry-visibility-bypass.name: fv-mov-2-cl3-entry-visibility-bypass
fv-mov-2-cl3-entry-visibility-bypass.description: A function declared public(package) entry is intended to be callable only within the package, but the entry modifier allows it to be called directly from any transaction. The entry keyword overrides the public(package) restriction, turning an internal function into public attack surface.

fv-mov-2-cl4-sender-spoofing.name: fv-mov-2-cl4-sender-spoofing
fv-mov-2-cl4-sender-spoofing.description: A function accepts a sender: address parameter to determine the caller's identity, rather than deriving it from txcontext::sender(ctx). Any caller can spoof any address by passing a victim's address, enabling them to perform operations on the victim's behalf.

fv-mov-3-cl1-init-upgrade-assumptions.name: fv-mov-3-cl1-init-upgrade-assumptions
fv-mov-3-cl1-init-upgrade-assumptions.description: In Sui Move, the init function runs only once at first deployment. Package upgrades do NOT re-execute init. Code that relies on init running again to reset state, create new capabilities, or initialize new fields will leave post-upgrade state uninitialized.

fv-mov-3-cl2-version-check-missing.name: fv-mov-3-cl2-version-check-missing
fv-mov-3-cl2-version-check-missing.description: After a package upgrade, old transactions may still call functions from the pre-upgrade package against existing shared objects. Without a version field and a per-function version assertion, old and new code can interleave, producing incompatible state transitions.

fv-mov-3-cl3-struct-field-evolution.name: fv-mov-3-cl3-struct-field-evolution
fv-mov-3-cl3-struct-field-evolution.description: Sui Move enforces forward-compatible struct evolution: fields may only be appended, never reordered or removed. Violating this rule causes existing on-chain objects (created by the old code) to fail deserialization when accessed by the new code.

fv-mov-3-cl4-upgrade-cap-security.name: fv-mov-3-cl4-upgrade-cap-security
fv-mov-3-cl4-upgrade-cap-security.description: The UpgradeCap for a Sui package is the single object controlling all future code upgrades. A compromised or malicious holder can deploy arbitrary new code, immediately draining all protocol funds. This is the highest-impact single point of failure in any upgradeable Sui protocol.

fv-mov-4-cl1-shared-object-races.name: fv-mov-4-cl1-shared-object-races
fv-mov-4-cl1-shared-object-races.description: Concurrent transactions targeting the same shared object can interleave reads and writes without a version or sequence check. The second writer overwrites the first writer's result, causing lost updates - for example, two deposits each read total = 100, add their amounts independently, and both writ

fv-mov-4-cl2-hot-potato-flash-loan.name: fv-mov-4-cl2-hot-potato-flash-loan
fv-mov-4-cl2-hot-potato-flash-loan.description: The hot potato pattern enforces flash loan repayment by making the receipt struct have no abilities - the compiler requires it to be consumed in the same PTB. Two failure modes: (1) receipt struct has drop or store ability, breaking enforcement; (2) receipt does not bind to the originating pool ID,

fv-mov-4-cl3-ptb-price-manipulation.name: fv-mov-4-cl3-ptb-price-manipulation
fv-mov-4-cl3-ptb-price-manipulation.description: Sui PTBs allow up to 1024 operations in one atomic transaction. An attacker can compose: (1) borrow via flash loan, (2) manipulate an on-chain price oracle or pool reserve ratio, (3) call the vulnerable function at the manipulated price, (4) repay the flash loan - all within a single transaction. Th

fv-mov-4-cl4-clock-and-time.name: fv-mov-4-cl4-clock-and-time
fv-mov-4-cl4-clock-and-time.description: Sui provides reliable on-chain time via clock::timestampms(&clock), which returns time in milliseconds. fv-mov-5-cl1-bitwise-and-custom-math.name: fv-mov-5-cl1-bitwise-and-custom-math
fv-mov-5-cl1-bitwise-and-custom-math.description: Move checks standard arithmetic overflow and aborts, but bitwise left-shift (<<) is NOT checked - it silently overflows. This vector directly caused the Cetus $223M exploit: a checkedshlw function had an incorrect shift limit (256 instead of 192), allowing the shift to overflow and produce a near-ze

fv-mov-5-cl2-division-and-underflow.name: fv-mov-5-cl2-division-and-underflow
fv-mov-5-cl2-division-and-underflow.description: Move has no floating-point types. Early division truncates precision: (amount / total) price can round to zero for small amounts, enabling dust exploits. Division by zero causes an abort, which can permanently DoS critical operations. Subtraction without a bounds check aborts on underflow in debug,

fv-mov-5-cl3-cast-truncation.name: fv-mov-5-cl3-cast-truncation
fv-mov-5-cl3-cast-truncation.description: Unlike standard arithmetic, Move's type casts (value as u64, value as u8) silently truncate high bits without aborting. A u128 value of 2^64 + 100 cast to u64 becomes 100, bypassing amount checks. This is distinct from arithmetic overflow - Move aborts on arithmetic overflow but not on cast truncati

fv-mov-5-cl4-rounding-and-constants.name: fv-mov-5-cl4-rounding-and-constants
fv-mov-5-cl4-rounding-and-constants.description: Vault and share protocols must round against the user to prevent slow pool drain: deposits should issue fewer shares (round down), withdrawals should return fewer tokens (round up). First-depositor vault inflation exploits the absence of virtual shares. Hardcoded constants with wrong digit counts (M

fv-mov-6-cl1-coin-balance-confusion.name: fv-mov-6-cl1-coin-balance-confusion
fv-mov-6-cl1-coin-balance-confusion.description: Sui separates Coin<T (an object with a UID, transferable) from Balance<T (an internal primitive value without an object ID). Mixing these without consistent accounting creates ghost balances - coins exist on-chain with no internal tracking, or internal counters exceed actual coins held.

fv-mov-6-cl2-supply-invariant-violations.name: fv-mov-6-cl2-supply-invariant-violations
fv-mov-6-cl2-supply-invariant-violations.description: Token/share supply must remain invariant: every mint has a corresponding deposit, every burn releases the corresponding asset. Violations include minting shares without receiving tokens, burning tokens without releasing collateral, and allowing self-transfers that trigger fee/reward snapshots withou

fv-mov-6-cl3-fee-accounting.name: fv-mov-6-cl3-fee-accounting
fv-mov-6-cl3-fee-accounting.description: Fee bypass occurs when an alternate code path (emergency withdraw, admin withdraw, batch operation) skips the fee calculation. Non-atomic fee deduction allows a PTB to skip the fee step. Missing fee withdrawal function locks protocol revenue permanently.

fv-mov-6-cl4-dust-and-cleanup.name: fv-mov-6-cl4-dust-and-cleanup
fv-mov-6-cl4-dust-and-cleanup.description: Three related cleanup failures: (1) tiny token amounts ("dust") prevent object closure, enabling attacker to permanently lock victim accounts; (2) parent objects deleted without removing dynamic fields, permanently orphaning stored values; (3) balance::destroyzero called on a potentially non-zero ba

fv-mov-8-cl1-generic-type-confusion.name: fv-mov-8-cl1-generic-type-confusion
fv-mov-8-cl1-generic-type-confusion.description: Unvalidated generic type parameters are the number-one critical vulnerability across real Move audits. An attacker creates a worthless Coin<FakeUSDC and passes it to any function accepting Coin<T without type validation, borrowing real assets against fake collateral. Phantom types on generic capabil

fv-mov-8-cl2-table-collection-bugs.name: fv-mov-8-cl2-table-collection-bugs
fv-mov-8-cl2-table-collection-bugs.description: table::add aborts on duplicate keys - missing existence checks cause DoS when a user interacts a second time. Move vectors are limited to ~1000 entries - unbounded vectors DoS when full. Both create permanent denial-of-service.

fv-mov-8-cl3-flash-loan-receipt-binding.name: fv-mov-8-cl3-flash-loan-receipt-binding
fv-mov-8-cl3-flash-loan-receipt-binding.description: Two confirmed critical flash loan findings from real audits: (1) receipt struct has no poolid field - repay function accepts receipts from Pool A to settle loans from Pool B (Cetus, Dexlyn); (2) flash loan start callable multiple times in the same PTB - second call resets the balance snapshot so fin

fv-mov-8-cl4-real-world-exploits.name: fv-mov-8-cl4-real-world-exploits
fv-mov-8-cl4-real-world-exploits.description: Three real-world High/Critical patterns: (1) multi-return functions with same-type values returned in wrong order - silently corrupts all callers (KriyaDEX getreserves); (2) assert!(x == x) tautology - always passes, validates nothing (Hop Aggregator version check); (3) reward accumulator updated af

fv-sol-1-c1-single-function.name: fv-sol-1-c1-single-function
fv-sol-1-c1-single-function.description: A single function performs an external call before updating its own state. An attacker's receive or fallback function re-enters the same function before the state change lands, allowing repeated withdrawal of the same balance within one transaction.

fv-sol-1-c2-cross-function.name: fv-sol-1-c2-cross-function
fv-sol-1-c2-cross-function.description: Multiple functions within the same contract share a state variable. One function makes an external call before updating that variable, while another function relies on the same variable for access control or accounting. An attacker re-enters the second function during the callback window to exploit

fv-sol-1-c3-cross-contract.name: fv-sol-1-c3-cross-contract
fv-sol-1-c3-cross-contract.description: An attacker deploys a dedicated malicious contract that acts as msg.sender and re-enters the victim contract during an external call callback. fv-sol-1-c4-cross-chain.name: fv-sol-1-c4-cross-chain
fv-sol-1-c4-cross-chain.description: Cross-chain reentrancy exploits the absence of replay protection and access control on bridge completion functions. fv-sol-1-c5-dynamic.name: fv-sol-1-c5-dynamic

fv-sol-1-c6-read-only.name: fv-sol-1-c6-read-only
fv-sol-1-c6-read-only.description: Read-only reentrancy occurs when a view function or an eligibility/price-check is called inside a state-modifying function after an external call. fv-sol-1-c7-erc721-erc1155-callback.name: fv-sol-1-c7-erc721-erc1155-callback
fv-sol-1-c7-erc721-erc1155-callback.description: safeTransferFrom, safeMint, and batch ERC1155 transfers invoke receiver callbacks (onERC721Received, onERC1155Received, onERC1155BatchReceived) before the calling contract has finished updating state. This enables reentrancy through the callback.

fv-sol-1-c8-erc777-hook-reentrancy.name: fv-sol-1-c8-erc777-hook-reentrancy
fv-sol-1-c8-erc777-hook-reentrancy.description: ERC777 tokens are backward-compatible with ERC20 but fire tokensToSend (on sender) and tokensReceived (on recipient) hooks via the ERC1820 registry on every transfer, including ERC20-style transfer() and transferFrom(). fv-sol-1-c9-transient-storage-reentrancy.name: fv-sol-1-c9-transient-storage-reentrancy
fv-sol-1-c9-transient-storage-reentrancy.description: Two reentrancy risks introduced by EIP-1153 (Cancun, March 2024): first, the classic transfer()/send() 2300-gas reentrancy guard is bypassed because TSTORE costs only 100 gas, allowing a receive() fallback to write transient state and re-enter within the gas limit. fv-sol-10-c1-incorrect-compounding-mecha.name: fv-sol-10-c1-incorrect-compounding-mechanism
fv-sol-10-c1-incorrect-compounding-mecha.description: Oracle price is used as a direct multiplier in interest or yield compounding logic without validation. An attacker who can influence the oracle can inflate or deflate the calculated interest in a single call, permanently distorting the cumulative value.

fv-sol-10-c2-price-drift.name: fv-sol-10-c2-price-drift
fv-sol-10-c2-price-drift.description: An oracle price that drifts gradually from reality causes cumulative accounting errors that compound over time. fv-sol-10-c3-manipulation-through-extern.name: fv-sol-10-c3-manipulation-through-external-markets
fv-sol-10-c3-manipulation-through-extern.description: Oracles that aggregate prices from low-liquidity external markets (DEXes, AMMs) can be temporarily skewed within a single block or flash loan transaction. A protocol using such a price without smoothing or secondary validation executes collateral, liquidation, or swap logic at the manipulated value.

fv-sol-10-c4-time-lags.name: fv-sol-10-c4-time-lags
fv-sol-10-c4-time-lags.description: Delaying block production or influencing the timing of oracle updates causes the price feed to serve stale data. Protocols that accept arbitrarily old prices expose themselves to exploitation using valuations that no longer reflect market reality - an attacker can front-run the staleness window to l

fv-sol-10-c5-chainlink-feed-validity.name: fv-sol-10-c5-chainlink-feed-validity
fv-sol-10-c5-chainlink-feed-validity.description: latestRoundData() returns multiple fields that must all be validated. fv-sol-10-c6-l2-sequencer-uptime.name: fv-sol-10-c6-l2-sequencer-uptime
fv-sol-10-c6-l2-sequencer-uptime.description: On L2 networks (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, and others), Chainlink price feeds continue to serve the last known price during sequencer downtime. fv-sol-10-c7-missing-price-bounds.name: fv-sol-10-c7-missing-price-bounds
fv-sol-10-c7-missing-price-bounds.description: An oracle can return a technically valid price - passing all staleness, round, and sign checks - that is wildly wrong for protocol purposes, such as during a flash crash or when a Chainlink circuit breaker activates. fv-sol-2-c1-token-decimals.name: fv-sol-2-c1-token-decimals
fv-sol-2-c1-token-decimals.description: Precision errors occur when contracts hardcode a decimal assumption (commonly 18) rather than reading the token's actual decimals() value. fv-sol-2-c2-floating-point.name: fv-sol-2-c2-floating-point
fv-sol-2-c2-floating-point.description: Solidity has no native floating-point type. The error compounds across repeated calculations and

fv-sol-2-c3-rounding.name: fv-sol-2-c3-rounding
fv-sol-2-c3-rounding.description: Solidity performs integer division with truncation (floor rounding toward zero), which silently discards fractional remainders. In contracts that distribute funds, accrue rewards, or compute fees across many users or iterations, these per-operation losses accumulate into meaningful discrepancies - e

fv-sol-2-c4-division-by-zero.name: fv-sol-2-c4-division-by-zero
fv-sol-2-c4-division-by-zero.description: Division by zero in Solidity causes an unconditional revert since 0.8.x (via the built-in overflow/underflow checks) or silent undefined behavior in earlier versions. fv-sol-2-c5-time-based.name: fv-sol-2-c5-time-based
fv-sol-2-c5-time-based.description: Contracts that use block.timestamp for fund release, access control, or randomness are exposed to two distinct risks: miner (or validator) manipulation of the timestamp by up to approximately 12-15 seconds per block, and the imprecision of treating a monotonically-increasing but not strictly-regular

fv-sol-2-c6-erc4626-rounding.name: fv-sol-2-c6-erc4626-rounding
fv-sol-2-c6-erc4626-rounding.description: EIP-4626 mandates specific rounding directions on every conversion function to prevent share-price manipulation and round-trip profit extraction. The invariant is: the vault must favor itself over the user at every step.

fv-sol-2-c7-special-token-accounting.name: fv-sol-2-c7-special-token-accounting
fv-sol-2-c7-special-token-accounting.description: Three related token behaviors break standard balance accounting assumptions: fee-on-transfer tokens deduct a fee during transferFrom so the contract records more than it received; rebasing tokens (stETH, AMPL, aTokens) change balanceOf over time without any transfer so cached balances go stale; and

fv-sol-3-c1-overflow-and-underflow.name: fv-sol-3-c1-overflow-and-underflow
fv-sol-3-c1-overflow-and-underflow.description: Integer overflow and underflow occur when arithmetic results exceed or drop below the bounds of the integer type. fv-sol-3-c2-sign-extension.name: fv-sol-3-c2-sign-extension
fv-sol-3-c2-sign-extension.description: Sign extension issues occur when a smaller signed integer type is implicitly or explicitly cast to a larger signed integer type. fv-sol-3-c3-truncation-in-type-casting.name: fv-sol-3-c3-truncation-in-type-casting

fv-sol-3-c4-misuse-of-environment-variab.name: fv-sol-3-c4-misuse-of-environment-variables
fv-sol-3-c4-misuse-of-environment-variab.description: Environment variables such as block.timestamp, block.number, and block.basefee carry miner- or validator-influenced values that should not be used as precise inputs to arithmetic or access control. fv-sol-3-c5-assembly-arithmetic.name: fv-sol-3-c5-assembly-arithmetic
fv-sol-3-c5-assembly-arithmetic.description: Arithmetic inside assembly {} (Yul) does not benefit from Solidity 0.8's checked math. fv-sol-3-c6-assembly-memory-calldata-pit.name: fv-sol-3-c6-assembly-memory-calldata-pitfalls
fv-sol-3-c6-assembly-memory-calldata-pit.description: Inline assembly bypasses Solidity's memory safety guarantees. fv-sol-4-c1-using-tx-origin-for-authoriz.name: fv-sol-4-c1-using-tx-origin-for-authorization

fv-sol-4-c10-commit-reveal-merkle-bindin.name: fv-sol-4-c10-commit-reveal-merkle-binding

Single-hashed leav

fv-sol-4-c11-hash-collision-and-encoding.name: fv-sol-4-c11-hash-collision-and-encoding
fv-sol-4-c11-hash-collision-and-encoding.description: Two encoding bugs allow attackers to produce colliding hashes or bypass deduplication. When abi.encodePacked is used with two or more dynamic-type arguments, inputs with different field boundaries but identical concatenated bytes produce the same hash. When protocols deduplicate by hashing raw msg.d

fv-sol-4-c2-unrestricted-role-assignment.name: fv-sol-4-c2-unrestricted-role-assignment
fv-sol-4-c2-unrestricted-role-assignment.description: When a function that assigns ownership, admin rights, or privileged roles is public and lacks any access control guard, any caller can elevate their own privileges or assign them to an attacker-controlled address, taking full control of the contract.

fv-sol-4-c3-lack-of-multi-signature-for-.name: fv-sol-4-c3-lack-of-multi-signature-for-crucial-operations
fv-sol-4-c3-lack-of-multi-signature-for-.description: When a single address controls a critical operation - such as draining contract funds, upgrading implementation logic, or changing protocol parameters - that address is a single point of failure. Compromise, loss, or coercion of that one key results in irreversible protocol damage with no recourse.

fv-sol-4-c4-signature-security-flaws.name: fv-sol-4-c4-signature-security-flaws
fv-sol-4-c4-signature-security-flaws.description: Signature-based authentication is vulnerable to three related issues: malleability (the same signing key produces two valid signatures for the same message), zero-address recovery (ecrecover returns address(0) for malformed signatures), and replay attacks (a valid signature used once can be reused).

fv-sol-4-c5-callback-authorization-bypas.name: fv-sol-4-c5-callback-authorization-bypass
fv-sol-4-c5-callback-authorization-bypas.description: External callback functions (onFlashLoan, onERC721Received, onERC1155Received) are invoked by third-party contracts. If the callback does not verify msg.sender is the expected caller, anyone can invoke it directly with fabricated parameters, bypassing intended access control. ERC4626 withdraw/redeem

fv-sol-4-c6-arbitrary-external-call.name: fv-sol-4-c6-arbitrary-external-call
fv-sol-4-c6-arbitrary-external-call.description: When a contract executes target.call{value: v}(data) where target or data are caller-supplied, an attacker can craft parameters to invoke unintended functions on any target contract. Common impact includes draining ERC20 allowances the contract holds, invoking transferFrom on behalf of the contract,

fv-sol-4-c7-erc1271-signature-delegation.name: fv-sol-4-c7-erc1271-signature-delegation
fv-sol-4-c7-erc1271-signature-delegation.description: ERC-1271 allows smart contract accounts to validate signatures by implementing isValidSignature(bytes32 hash, bytes calldata signature) returns (bytes4). When a protocol relies on this for authorization and the implementation delegates to an externally-supplied or insufficiently-guarded module, a ma

fv-sol-4-c8-arbitrary-storage-write.name: fv-sol-4-c8-arbitrary-storage-write
fv-sol-4-c8-arbitrary-storage-write.description: Two distinct patterns allow writing to arbitrary storage slots: inline assembly sstore(slot, value) where the slot is derived from user input without bounds checking, and in Solidity < 0.6, direct assignment to array.length combined with a crafted large index causes slot arithmetic to wrap, writing

fv-sol-4-c9-constructor-bypass-and-creat.name: fv-sol-4-c9-constructor-bypass-and-create2-squatting
fv-sol-4-c9-constructor-bypass-and-creat.description: Two related patterns allow attackers to bypass access controls that assume msg.sender is an EOA or a not-yet-deployed address. During construction, extcodesize is zero even though the caller is a contract, allowing constructor-context calls to pass EOA-only guards. With CREATE2, if the salt is not b

fv-sol-5-c1-boundary-misalignment.name: fv-sol-5-c1-boundary-misalignment
fv-sol-5-c1-boundary-misalignment.description: Occurs when code fails to correctly define exclusive versus inclusive boundaries at interval thresholds, causing values at the cutoff to fall into the wrong range, be double-counted, or be skipped entirely.

fv-sol-5-c10-data-structure-state-integr.name: fv-sol-5-c10-data-structure-state-integrity
fv-sol-5-c10-data-structure-state-integr.description: Three related patterns where data structure operations leave inconsistent state:

fv-sol-5-c11-weak-onchain-randomness.name: fv-sol-5-c11-weak-onchain-randomness
fv-sol-5-c11-weak-onchain-randomness.description: Randomness derived from on-chain values is manipulable by validators/miners or predictable by any caller, making it unsuitable for games, lotteries, NFT trait generation, or any outcome where a participant can gain an advantage by knowing the result in advance.

fv-sol-5-c2-incorrect-conditionals.name: fv-sol-5-c2-incorrect-conditionals
fv-sol-5-c2-incorrect-conditionals.description: Results from conditions in if-else chains where more specific cases are tested after more general ones, making specific branches unreachable, or from wrong comparison operators that cause values to be handled by the wrong branch or skipped entirely.

fv-sol-5-c3-improper-state-transitions.name: fv-sol-5-c3-improper-state-transitions
fv-sol-5-c3-improper-state-transitions.description: A contract with a defined lifecycle (e.g., NotStarted, Active, Paused, Completed) allows state-modifying functions to execute without validating the current state, permitting out-of-order or repeated transitions that violate invariants and can be exploited.

fv-sol-5-c4-misordered-calculations.name: fv-sol-5-c4-misordered-calculations
fv-sol-5-c4-misordered-calculations.description: Arithmetic operations applied in the wrong sequence produce incorrect results. Common cases include applying a bonus before a tax so the bonus is also taxed, computing interest before updating the principal, or applying a percentage to a post-adjusted value when the specification requires it on the

fv-sol-5-c5-event-misreporting.name: fv-sol-5-c5-event-misreporting
fv-sol-5-c5-event-misreporting.description: Events emit incorrect values - such as a cumulative balance instead of the current operation amount - causing off-chain indexers, monitoring systems, and oracles to record wrong data while on-chain state may be correct.

fv-sol-5-c6-same-block-snapshot-abuse.name: fv-sol-5-c6-same-block-snapshot-abuse
fv-sol-5-c6-same-block-snapshot-abuse.description: Protocols that calculate yield, rewards, voting power, or insurance coverage based on a balance snapshot at a single point in time are vulnerable to flash loan amplification. An attacker borrows tokens, deposits before the snapshot (or in the same block), claims the benefit, then repays - all in one

fv-sol-5-c7-msg-value-reuse-multicall.name: fv-sol-5-c7-msg-value-reuse-multicall
fv-sol-5-c7-msg-value-reuse-multicall.description: msg.value is a global that persists for the entire transaction. Reading it inside a loop or inside delegatecall-based multicall credits the full original ETH value on every iteration - a single payment appears as N payments.

fv-sol-5-c8-force-eth-injection.name: fv-sol-5-c8-force-eth-injection
fv-sol-5-c8-force-eth-injection.description: Three mechanisms send ETH to a contract without triggering receive() or fallback():

fv-sol-5-c9-deployment-config-pitfalls.name: fv-sol-5-c9-deployment-config-pitfalls
fv-sol-5-c9-deployment-config-pitfalls.description: Errors in deployment scripts and contract configuration cause permanent misconfiguration or front-runnable initialization windows. These are not runtime logic bugs but deployment-time failures that are often irrecoverable.

fv-sol-6-c1-unchecked-call-return.name: fv-sol-6-c1-unchecked-call-return
fv-sol-6-c1-unchecked-call-return.description: Low-level calls (call, delegatecall, staticcall, send) return a boolean success flag instead of reverting on failure. When the return value is discarded the caller continues execution under the false assumption that the operation succeeded, enabling lost funds, skipped logic, and corrupted state.

fv-sol-6-c10-nonstandard-erc20-behavior.name: fv-sol-6-c10-nonstandard-erc20-behavior
fv-sol-6-c10-nonstandard-erc20-behavior.description: Several widely-used tokens deviate from the ERC20 spec in ways that break standard protocol integration:

fv-sol-6-c11-create-deployment-silent-fa.name: fv-sol-6-c11-create-deployment-silent-failure
fv-sol-6-c11-create-deployment-silent-fa.description: Assembly create(v, offset, size) and create2(v, offset, size, salt) return address(0) on failure - insufficient ETH balance, address collision, or init code revert. Unlike the high-level new Contract() syntax, these opcodes do not revert automatically on failure.

fv-sol-6-c2-unchecked-transfer-return.name: fv-sol-6-c2-unchecked-transfer-return
fv-sol-6-c2-unchecked-transfer-return.description: Failing to check the return value of transfer or transferFrom on ERC20 tokens allows silent transfer failures to go undetected. Certain tokens return false instead of reverting on failure; ignoring the return value lets execution continue as if the transfer succeeded, leading to incorrect balance ac

fv-sol-6-c3-silent-fail.name: fv-sol-6-c3-silent-fail
fv-sol-6-c3-silent-fail.description: A function call fails without detection and execution continues as if it succeeded, producing an invalid or inconsistent contract state. This pattern arises whenever a callee signals failure through a return value rather than a revert and the caller does not inspect that value.

fv-sol-6-c4-false-positive-success-assum.name: fv-sol-6-c4-false-positive-success-assumption
fv-sol-6-c4-false-positive-success-assum.description: The contract captures a failure signal from an external call but treats the failure path as a no-op, allowing execution to continue as if the call succeeded. This produces state inconsistencies and incorrect balance or permission assumptions when the external call actually failed.

fv-sol-6-c5-partial-execution-with-no-ro.name: fv-sol-6-c5-partial-execution-with-no-rollback
fv-sol-6-c5-partial-execution-with-no-ro.description: When an external call fails mid-function, prior state mutations already applied in the same transaction are not automatically rolled back unless the function reverts. Manual compensation logic is error-prone and may leave state partially modified, producing inconsistencies that compound over subsequ

fv-sol-6-c6-false-contract-existence-ass.name: fv-sol-6-c6-false-contract-existence-assumption
fv-sol-6-c6-false-contract-existence-ass.description: Calling a function on an address that contains no contract code does not revert - the EVM treats it as a successful call returning empty data. When a protocol stores or accepts an external address without verifying it is a deployed contract, calls to that address silently succeed as no-ops, producin

fv-sol-6-c7-zero-amount-transfer-revert.name: fv-sol-6-c7-zero-amount-transfer-revert
fv-sol-6-c7-zero-amount-transfer-revert.description: Some non-standard ERC20 tokens (LEND, early BNB, and others) revert on transfer(to, 0) or transferFrom(from, to, 0). Protocols that perform distribution loops or yield claims without guarding against zero amounts will be DoS'd when the distributed amount rounds to zero - permanently bricking claims

fv-sol-6-c8-return-bomb.name: fv-sol-6-c8-return-bomb
fv-sol-6-c8-return-bomb.description: When a contract makes an external call using (bool success, bytes memory data) = target.call(payload), the EVM copies the full returndata into memory. A malicious or compromised target can return enormous amounts of data, causing the caller to spend enormous gas copying it - potentially exceeding th

fv-sol-6-c9-erc721-unsafe-transfer.name: fv-sol-6-c9-erc721-unsafe-transfer
fv-sol-6-c9-erc721-unsafe-transfer.description: ERC721.transfer() and the low-level transferFrom() do not check whether the recipient contract implements IERC721Receiver. Sending an NFT to a contract that lacks the receiver interface permanently locks the token - it can never be recovered.

fv-sol-7-c1-delegatecall-storage-collisi.name: fv-sol-7-c1-delegatecall-storage-collision
fv-sol-7-c1-delegatecall-storage-collisi.description: delegatecall executes code from another contract in the calling contract's storage context, preserving msg.sender and msg.value. When the proxy and implementation contracts declare state variables at overlapping storage slots, writes from the implementation silently corrupt proxy-level state such as

fv-sol-7-c2-function-selector-collision.name: fv-sol-7-c2-function-selector-collision
fv-sol-7-c2-function-selector-collision.description: Function selectors are the first four bytes of the keccak256 hash of a function signature. When a proxy contract exposes public functions whose selectors match functions in the implementation, the proxy intercepts and handles those calls itself rather than delegating them, causing silent misbehavior

fv-sol-7-c3-centralized-update-control.name: fv-sol-7-c3-centralized-update-control
fv-sol-7-c3-centralized-update-control.description: When upgrade authority is held by a single EOA or unconstrained admin address, a compromised or malicious key holder can replace the implementation with arbitrary code, draining funds or bricking the contract. This represents a critical trust assumption that undermines the security guarantees of the

fv-sol-7-c4-uninitialized-proxy.name: fv-sol-7-c4-uninitialized-proxy
fv-sol-7-c4-uninitialized-proxy.description: Proxy contracts that use initialize() instead of constructors for setup can be left in an uninitialized state if the initializer is never called, or can be re-initialized if the initializer lacks a one-time-use guard. Either condition allows an attacker to set critical ownership or configuration var

fv-sol-7-c5-proxy-implementation-attacks.name: fv-sol-7-c5-proxy-implementation-attacks
fv-sol-7-c5-proxy-implementation-attacks.description: Implementation contracts are not just storage targets - they are execution contexts with their own attack surface. Vulnerabilities include immutable variable context mismatch across proxies, arbitrary delegatecall exposed in the implementation, incomplete assembly fallback propagation, minimal proxy

fv-sol-7-c6-proxy-upgrade-lifecycle.name: fv-sol-7-c6-proxy-upgrade-lifecycle
fv-sol-7-c6-proxy-upgrade-lifecycle.description: The upgrade lifecycle - initialization, authorization, and execution ordering - has several critical failure modes including re-initialization via wrong modifier, permanent loss of upgrade capability when UUPS logic is dropped, race conditions between upgrade and configuration, missing access contro

fv-sol-7-c7-diamond-proxy-pitfalls.name: fv-sol-7-c7-diamond-proxy-pitfalls
fv-sol-7-c7-diamond-proxy-pitfalls.description: EIP-2535 Diamond proxies introduce unique storage and selector collision risks beyond standard proxy patterns. Facets that declare top-level state variables all start at slot 0, overwriting each other's data. Adding a facet with a selector that already exists in another facet hijacks all calls to th

fv-sol-8-c1-price-manipulation.name: fv-sol-8-c1-price-manipulation
fv-sol-8-c1-price-manipulation.description: Relying solely on a DEX's own spot price to validate or derive swap parameters allows an attacker to manipulate the pool state (via flash loan or large trade) immediately before the victim transaction, causing extreme slippage. Without cross-referencing an external or time-weighted price, the contra

fv-sol-8-c2-front-running.name: fv-sol-8-c2-front-running
fv-sol-8-c2-front-running.description: Swap transactions published to the public mempool expose their parameters - token pair, input amount, and minimum output - before inclusion. MEV bots observe these parameters and sandwich the victim: a buy is inserted before the transaction to move the price up, and a sell is inserted after, extract

fv-sol-8-c3-insufficient-liquidity.name: fv-sol-8-c3-insufficient-liquidity
fv-sol-8-c3-insufficient-liquidity.description: When a DEX pool has insufficient liquidity relative to the swap size, price impact grows non-linearly and the resulting output can be drastically below fair value. Without a pre-swap liquidity check or a tightly enforced amountOutMinimum, the contract accepts any output the pool returns, including n

fv-sol-8-c4-unexpected-gas-increase.name: fv-sol-8-c4-unexpected-gas-increase
fv-sol-8-c4-unexpected-gas-increase.description: When a swap wrapper forwards execution to an external DEX without a gas cap, an attacker or a malicious/upgraded DEX implementation can consume unbounded gas. This drives up transaction costs, can cause out-of-gas reverts for the user, or - in protocols that deduct gas costs from the output amount -

fv-sol-8-c5-missing-deadline.name: fv-sol-8-c5-missing-deadline
fv-sol-8-c5-missing-deadline.description: Without a meaningful deadline, a swap transaction can be held in the mempool indefinitely by validators and executed at an arbitrary future time when conditions may be unfavorable. deadline = block.timestamp is always valid (the transaction executes in the same block it appears to be submitted), and

fv-sol-8-c6-oracle-price-update-frontrun.name: fv-sol-8-c6-oracle-price-update-frontrunning
fv-sol-8-c6-oracle-price-update-frontrun.description: Push-model oracle integrations (Chainlink push, custom off-chain updater submitting to public mempool) expose the price update transaction before it lands. An attacker who sees a favorable update in the mempool can front-run it: open a position at the stale price, let the update land, then profit fr

fv-sol-9-c1-dynamic-array.name: fv-sol-9-c1-dynamic-array
fv-sol-9-c1-dynamic-array.description: Loops that iterate over a dynamic array whose length grows with user-controlled input have unbounded gas cost. As the array grows, any function performing a full iteration will eventually exceed the block gas limit and revert permanently.

fv-sol-9-c2-unrestricted-mapping.name: fv-sol-9-c2-unrestricted-mapping
fv-sol-9-c2-unrestricted-mapping.description: Solidity mappings cannot be iterated natively, so developers often maintain a parallel array of keys. If this auxiliary array grows without restriction, any function that loops over it to aggregate or process mapping values will eventually exceed the block gas limit.

fv-sol-9-c3-recursive-calls.name: fv-sol-9-c3-recursive-calls
fv-sol-9-c3-recursive-calls.description: Solidity imposes a call-stack depth limit of 1024 frames. Recursive self-calls or chains of delegating function calls that scale with user-supplied input will exhaust the call stack or gas budget before completing. Even when disguised as iterative withdrawal logic, each self-call consumes additional

fv-sol-9-c4-reentrancy-loops.name: fv-sol-9-c4-reentrancy-loops
fv-sol-9-c4-reentrancy-loops.description: Loops that perform external calls on each iteration compound two risks: unbounded gas cost from the iteration itself, and reentrancy from any external call within the loop body. A malicious recipient can re-enter the looping function mid-iteration, causing state corruption, double-spending, or out-o

fv-sol-9-c5-nested-loops.name: fv-sol-9-c5-nested-loops
fv-sol-9-c5-nested-loops.description: Nested loops whose bounds are both determined by user-controlled data produce O(nm) gas costs. Even modest growth in either dimension can push the combined iteration count past the block gas limit, permanently bricking any function that relies on full traversal in a single transaction.

fv-sol-9-c6-blacklistable-token-payment.name: fv-sol-9-c6-blacklistable-token-payment
fv-sol-9-c6-blacklistable-token-payment.description: Push-model payment loops that transfer tokens to recipient addresses will revert entirely if any recipient is blacklisted by the token contract (USDC, USDT, and other compliant stablecoins support blacklisting). A single blacklisted address in a liquidation path, fee distribution loop, or withdrawal

fv-sol-9-c7-gas-griefing.name: fv-sol-9-c7-gas-griefing
fv-sol-9-c7-gas-griefing.description: Two related gas-based DoS patterns: block stuffing fills blocks with high-gas-price transactions to prevent time-sensitive protocol operations from executing within their window; the 63/64 rule allows a relayer to forward insufficient gas so the inner call silently fails while the outer call marks t

fv-sol-9-c8-dust-griefing.name: fv-sol-9-c8-dust-griefing
fv-sol-9-c8-dust-griefing.description: Two griefing patterns exploiting minimal-cost interactions: a dust deposit with no minimum amount can reset a per-user timelock indefinitely, and a dust token transfer to a contract can permanently block a zero-balance gate that guards a state transition.

algo-stables.name: algo-stables
algo-stables.description: Applies to: algorithmic stablecoins, rebase tokens, seigniorage stablecoins, uncollateralized stablecoins, Terra/LUNA-style, Ampleforth-style, peg maintained purely through mint/burn mechanics

bridges.description: Applies to: asset bridges, token bridges, cross-chain message passing, LayerZero integrations, Wormhole integrations, Axelar integrations, lock-and-mint bridges, burn-and-mint bridges, optimistic bridges

nft-gaming.name: nft-gaming
nft-gaming.description: Applies to: NFT marketplaces, NFT minting contracts, play-to-earn games, on-chain games, gamefi, NFT staking, trait-based NFTs, SeaDrop-style, OpenSea-style

nft-marketplace.description: Applies to: NFT marketplaces, order book marketplaces, Seaport-style, LooksRare-style, Blur-style, on-chain NFT auctions, NFT lending markets, ERC-721/ERC-1155 trading protocols

privacy.description: Applies to: privacy protocols, on-chain mixing, zero-knowledge proof systems, shielded pools, Tornado Cash-style, Aztec-style, zk-privacy applications
